newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso summons Motta for "a chat".
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso summons Motta for "a chat".

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso has called in Communications Minister Sergio Motta for "a chat" over controversial comments the minister made in news magazine Veja, a presidential spokesman said Monday.
"The president read the interview in Veja and did not like it," Cardoso's spokesman Sergio Amaral told reporters.
Motta, whose aggressive political style regularly lands him in hot water, cast aspersions on two ministers and several other government officials in an interview with Veja published Sunday.
The comments offended members of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) and the Brazilian Progressive Party (PPB), both of which are key members of the government's alliance.
"The president has ordered minister Sergio Motta in for a chat, either today or tomorrow," Amaral said.

In the interview, Motta said he was disappointed the appointment of leading members of the PMDB as Brazil's new transport and justice ministers had not resulted in increased support from the party for the government in Congress.
Another PDMB-sponsored appointment of the son of a construction company as the head of Minas Gerais state's highway department was "shameful," he said.
Motta also criticized the head of the state-run postal service, who was nominated by the PPB and suggested he might sack him.

With political party bosses fuming, government officials spent much of Monday trying to downplay Motta's comments. Planning Minister Antonio Kandir told reporters they were "just his way of expressing himself."
But that was not enough to prevent the president of the Brazilian Post and Telegraph Co from reportedly offering his resignation to his mentors in the PPB.

The uproar is the latest in a long string caused by Motta and his outspoken views. On the first day of Cardoso's government, he picked a fight with the president's former right-wing foes who are now his allies.

Since then, the minister has offended a host of public figures, ranging from Cardoso's wife to senior members of the Catholic Church. In April, the tables were turned when a newspaper claimed it had tapes of lawmakers talking about how Motta had bought their votes.
No hard proof came of the scandal, however, and Motta has defied his critics by remaining in his job, pressing on with Brazil's multi-billion-dollar plan to privatize its telecommunications industry.
